newsitem.title: GERMANY: BASF says U.S. lawsuit unfounded, grotesque.
newsitem.headline: BASF says U.S. lawsuit unfounded, grotesque.

text.p: German chemicals group BASF AG said Monday that an $8.5 billion lawsuit filed in a U.S. court against it and its Knoll Pharmaceutical Co. unit was unfounded.
"We regard the lawsuit as unfounded and the damages sought as grotesquely excessive," BASF spokesman Bernd Gerling said in response to an inquiry. He declined to comment further.

The lawsuit alleges that BASF, Knoll and Boots Pharmaceutical concealed a seven-year university study that concluded that their thyroid drug was no better than cheaper, generic brands to treat people suffering from hypothyroidism.
Boots Co. Plc, a retail pharmacy chain, issued a statement in London saying it was not a "proper defendant" in the case.

"The suggestion that Boots has been involved in any anti-trust or racketeering activity in connection with this matter is absurd and the idea that there may be multi-billion dollar liabilities involved is fanciful," Boots said in its statement.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in San Francisco. Attorney Barry Himmelstein, representing thyroid patients, said Saturday he would seek class action status for the suit and a jury trial in San Francisco.

An estimated 8 million Americans suffer from hypothyroidism, a condition caused by an under-active thyroid gland. The gland, located in the neck, produces a hormone called thyroxine, which regulates the body's metabolism. People with hypothyroidism must receive thyroxine in order to survive.

The vast majority of people with hypothyroidism take the drug Synthroid -- a synthetic version of the compound levothyroxine -- manufactured and sold by Boots and later by Knoll. Knoll now controls 84 percent of the $600 million a year levothyroxine market in the United States, the suit said.
A 1990 study by researchers at the University of California at San Francisco concluded that Synthroid was no more effective than less-expensive generic drugs.
The study, however, was not published for seven years because its sponsor, Boots Pharmaceutical, objected to the findings, the lawsuit alleged.
When the researchers told Boots they would publish their article anyway, the company invoked a clause in its contract with the university to block them from doing so.
In April 1995 Boots sold its drug division, which manufactured and sold Synthroid, to BASF, which incorporated the division into its Knoll subsidiary.

Under increased pressure from researchers and U.S. health officials, Knoll agreed in November 1996 not to prevent the San Francisco researchers from publishing their results. The study finally appeared in the Journal of the American Medical Association last month.
After it was published, Knoll said in a statement that it strongly disagreed with the validity of the study.
"The company believes that the study contains major flaws in design and execution, and fails to support the authors' conclusions," it said.
The federal lawsuit, filed on April 29, was first reported in the San Jose Mercury News on Saturday.

The lawsuit alleges that BASF, Knoll and Boots violated federal antitrust and racketeering laws when they suppressed the university study and forced millions of patients to buy their drug instead of less-expensive generic brands.
